<authenticate_cache_garbage_interval_explain>The time period between garbage collection across the username cache.[br]

 Only change if you have good reason to.
 </authenticate_cache_garbage_interval_explain>
<authenticate_ttl_explain>
The time a user and their credentials stay in the logged in user cache since their last request.[br]
When the garbage interval passes, all user credentials that have passed their TTL are removed from memory.
</authenticate_ttl_explain>
<authenticate_ip_ttl_explain>
If you use proxy authentication and the Max IP Per user ACL,this directive controls how long proxy remembers the IP addresses associated with each user.[br]Use a small value (e.g., 60 seconds) if your users might change addresses quickly, as is the case with dialup.[br]
You might be safe using a larger value (e.g., 2 hours) in a corporate LAN environment with relatively static address assignments.
</authenticate_ip_ttl_explain>
<credentialsttl_explain>
Specifies how long the proxy assumes an externally validated username:password pair is valid for.[br]
In other words how often the helper program is called for that user.[br]
Set this low to force revalidation with short lived passwords.
</credentialsttl_explain>

<explain_HaProxycD>The client did not send nor acknowledge any data for as long as the defined "timeout client" delay.[br]

<explain_HaProxysD>

 This is often caused by too short timeouts on L4 equipments before the server (firewalls,load-balancers, ...), as well as keep-alive sessions maintained between the client and the server expiring first on this load-balancer
</explain_HaProxysD>
<explain_HaProxyCD>The client unexpectedly aborted during data transfer.[br]

<zram_compressed_swap>Compressed Swap (zRam)</zram_compressed_swap>
<zram_enable>Enable zRam compressed swap</zram_enable>
<zram_size_percent>RAM percentage for zRam</zram_size_percent>
<zram_compression_ratio>Compression ratio</zram_compression_ratio>
<zram_space_saved>Space saved</zram_space_saved>
<zram_original_data>Original data</zram_original_data>
<zram_swap_usage>zRam swap usage</zram_swap_usage>
<zram_mem_efficiency>Memory efficiency</zram_mem_efficiency>
<zram_not_active>zRam is not active</zram_not_active>
<zram_explain>zRam creates a compressed swap area directly in your system's RAM instead of using the hard disk.[br]When the system needs to free memory, pages are compressed and stored in this reserved RAM area rather than being written to the slow disk-based swap partition.[br]Because data is compressed before storage, zRam typically achieves a 2:1 to 4:1 compression ratio.[br]This means 1 GB of RAM reserved for zRam can effectively hold 2 to 4 GB of swapped data, giving your system significantly more usable memory.[br]The main benefits are faster swap operations since RAM is hundreds of times faster than disk, reduced disk I/O which extends SSD lifespan, and improved overall system responsiveness under memory pressure.[br]The CPU cost for compression is minimal with the LZ4 algorithm.[br]zRam is particularly useful for systems running memory-intensive services like proxy caches, databases, or web filtering engines.[br]It allows the system to handle temporary memory spikes without the severe performance degradation that disk-based swapping causes.[br]</zram_explain>

<maxconn>Maximum number of connections</maxconn>
<haproxy_maxconn>By default, this parameter is set to 2000.[br]This means that a default instance of the load-balancer will start queuing HTTP sessions once it hits 2000 concurrent sessions.
</haproxy_maxconn>
<nbproc>Number of workers</nbproc>
<haproxy_nbproc>By default, the load-balancer service has a single worker process, which means that all of our HTTP sessions will be load balanced by a single process.[br]
 With the Number of workers parameter, it is possible to create multiple worker processes to help distribute the workload internally.[br]While additional worker processes might sound good at first, they only tend to provide value when the server itself has more than 1 CPU.[br]
 It is not uncommon for environments that create multiple worker processes on single CPU systems to see that the load-balancer performs worse than it did as a single process instance.[br]
 The reason for this is because the overhead of managing multiple worker processes provides a diminishing return when the number of workers exceeds the number of CPUs available.
</haproxy_nbproc>

<DNS_CAA_EXPLAIN>A Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) record is used to specify which certificate authorities (CAs) are allowed to issue certificates for a domain.[br]
CAA records allow domain owners to declare which certificate authorities are allowed to issue a certificate for a domain.[br]
They also provide a means of indicating notification rules in case someone requests a certificate from an unauthorized certificate authority.[br]
If no CAA record is present, any CA is allowed to issue a certificate for the domain.[br]
If a CAA record is present, only the CAs listed in the record(s) are allowed to issue certificates for that hostname.[br]
CAA records can set policy for the entire domain or for specific hostnames.[br]
CAA records are also inherited by subdomains</DNS_CAA_EXPLAIN>

<ospf_network_explain>
This section is a way of assigning an interface to a certain area.[br]
The mask is used as a shortcut and it helps putting a list of interfaces in the same area.[br]
The mask contains wild card bits where 0 is a match and 1 is a "do not care" bit, e.g. 0.0.255.255 indicates a match in the first two bytes of the network number.[br]
The area identifier is the area number we want the interface to be in.[br]
It can be an integer between 0 and 4294967295 or can take a form similar to an IP address A.B.C.D.</ospf_network_explain>

A Domain Name System-based blackhole list, Domain Name System blacklist (DNSBL) or real-time blackhole list (RBL) is a service for operation of mail servers to perform a check via a Domain Name System (DNS) query whether a sending host's IP address is blacklisted for email spam.[1] Most mail server software can be configured to check such lists, typically rejecting or flagging messages from such sites.
<dnsbl_explain>
A DNSBL is a software mechanism, rather than a specific list or policy.[br]
They use a wide array of criteria for listing and delisting addresses.[br]
These may include listing the addresses of zombie computers or other machines being used to send spam, Internet service providers (ISPs) who willingly host spammers, or those which have sent spam to a honeypot system.[br]
This section lists the open public reputation services that your server can query.[br]
Unlike The Shields which uses a dedicated reputation aggregation technology, these lists may have unwanted effects.
</dnsbl_explain>

<haproxy_timeout_connect>This timeout works like a grace period.[br]
It sets the maximum time the client has to connect to a server.[br]
The time it takes a client to connect to a server varies widely, depending on network complexity.[br]
The more complex a topology, the longer it can take the client to connect.[br]
The timeout connect allows the client to try to connect again if the initial attempt fails.[br]
 In addition to the connection time, you’ll need to set the numbers of retries.[br]
 The default is three, but you can adjust it to fit your environment.</haproxy_timeout_connect>
 <haproxy_timeout_server>
 When a client sends a request to the server, it expects a response.
[br]If the server doesn’t respond in the configured time duration, this paremeter is invoked.[br]
 This is akin to the timeout client, only in reverse.[br]
You can see in the list of HTTP responses, if a timeout server is invoked, you’ll get a 504 Gateway Timeout response from The Load-balancer.
</haproxy_timeout_server>
<haproxy_timeout_client>
This setting defines the maximum time a client can be inactive when connected to the server.[br]
 A common value for this timeout is five minutes.[br]
You can go with shorter timeouts, even as little as thirty seconds, if you’re attempting to maximize security or the total number of active connections.[br]
As the name suggests, this timeout is handled on the client side.
</haproxy_timeout_client>

<proxy_cache_revalidate>Revalidation of expired cache items</proxy_cache_revalidate>
<proxy_cache_revalidate_explain>Instructs the reverse-proxy to use conditional (GET) requests when refreshing content from the origin servers.[br]
If a client requests an item that is cached but expired as defined by the cache control headers, the reverse proxy includes the (If-Modified-Since) field in the header of the (GET) request it sends to the origin server.[br]This saves on bandwidth, because the server sends the full item only if it has been modified since the time recorded in the (Last-Modified) header attached to the file when the reverse-proxy originally cached it.
</proxy_cache_revalidate_explain>

<kernel_shmmax>Max shared memory</kernel_shmmax>
<kernel_shmmax_explain>This value defines the maximum size of a shared memory segment.[br]
This means that each shared memory segment cannot exceed this size.[br]
The size of each shared memory segment is important because it directly influences the performance of your system.[br]The par value is usually 4294967295 (4 GB) for 64-bit systems.[br]
It is important to note that this value should be less than or equal to half of the total physical memory size of your server.[br]It is recommended to set this value according to the size of the memory available on your server, if you have a large memory you can increase the value, otherwise it is better to leave it as it is to avoid performance problems.</kernel_shmmax_explain>
<kernel_shmall>Shared Memory</kernel_shmall>
<kernel_shmall_explain>
This value determines the total size of shared memory available for systems using System V shared memory.[br]
It is expressed in number of memory pages.[br]
You can increase it. [br]
However, it is important to note that this change will not increase the amount of physical memory available on your system.[br]
It will simply increase the amount of shared memory available for systems using System V shared memory.[br]
For example, if you have 8 GB of physical memory, you can calculate the value as follows:[br]
(8 * 1024 * 1024) / 4096.[br]
This gives 2,097,152, which is the value in number of pages.
</kernel_shmall_explain>

<ConcurrentDatabaseReload>Non-blocking database reloads</ConcurrentDatabaseReload>
<ConcurrentDatabaseReload_text>Enable non-blocking (multi-threaded/concurrent) database reloads.[br]
This feature will temporarily load a second scanning engine while scanning continues using the first engine.[br]
Once loaded, the new engine takes over.[br]
The old engine is removed as soon as all scans using the old engine have completed.[br]
This feature requires more RAM, so this option is provided in case users are willing to block scans during reload in exchange for lower RAM requirements.

<inbound_anomaly_score_threshold>Anomaly Score Threshold</inbound_anomaly_score_threshold>
<inbound_anomaly_score_threshold_explain>An anomaly score threshold is the cumulative anomaly score at which an inbound request or an outbound response will be blocked.[br]
Most detected inbound threats carry an anomaly score of 5 (by default), while smaller violations, e.g. protocol and standards violations, carry lower scores.[br]
An anomaly score threshold of 7, for example, would require multiple rule matches in order to trigger a block (e.g. one critical rule scoring 5 plus a lesser-scoring rule, in order to reach the threshold of 7).[br]An anomaly score threshold of 10 would require at least two critical rules to match, or a combination of many lesser-scoring rules.[br]
 Increasing the anomaly score thresholds makes the WAF less sensitive and hence less likely to block transactions.</inbound_anomaly_score_threshold_explain>

<proxy_transparent_wizard>Enabling transparent mode allows Artica to become a network gateway mode proxy.[br]
This mode eliminates the need to configure the proxy settings in the browser.[br]
A transparent proxy works by intercepting traffic directly at the network layer. In this configuration mode, Artica becomes an intermediate gateway for your network's Internet access.[br]
Consequently, it allows deploying the proxy even on devices not managed by the company.[br]
Once this option is enabled on Artica, you will have two options to deploy this mode of operation.[br]
The first option involves modifying the exit gateway in the DHCP server configuration.[br]
The second option involves performing TCP/IP routing of HTTP/HTTPS traffic to the network address of your transparent Artica server.[br]
 [br]In both scenarios, it is always recommended to secure the firewall at the exit of HTTP/HTTPS traffic to ensure that users cannot access the Internet without going through Artica.
</proxy_transparent_wizard>

<Kerberos_replay_cache>Kerberos Replay cache</Kerberos_replay_cache>
<Kerberos_replay_cache_explain>
Enabling the Kerberos replay cache (rcache) protects your service from token re-use (replay) attacks during authentication.[br]
In practice, it’s almost always worth having it on.
The server stores a fingerprint of each authenticator it accepts and rejects any duplicate until it expires (typically the clock-skew window, ~5 minutes).[br]
It’s per-host: it protects that machine from replays of recently seen tokens.[br]
[b]It Blocks stolen-token replays.[/b][br]
The AP-REQ authenticator (timestamp + key material) can be captured and reused by an attacker within the clock-skew window.[br] The cache records seen authenticators and rejects duplicates, stopping one-shot replays (common with HTTP Negotiate on proxies/reverse-proxies).[br]
[b]Prevents duplicate side-effects.[/b][br] Without cache, a replayed token could trigger the same authenticated action again (e.g., POST or admin call) even if no session is established yet.[br]
[b]Buys time before a full GSS context exists.[/b][br]
Many apps only perform the initial Kerberos exchange (no message signing yet).[br]Cache protects that early step.
</Kerberos_replay_cache_explain>

<enforce_user_dns_ttl>Enforce minimum TTL (client-visible)</enforce_user_dns_ttl>
<enforce_user_dns_ttl_explain>Ensure every DNS answer sent to clients has a TTL of at least [b]3600 seconds[/b], regardless of the upstream TTL or what’s stored in cache.[br]
When enabled, the DNS service rewrites low TTLs on the fly (both normal responses and cache hits) so clients will cache results for at least one hour.[br]
[b]Notes:[/b][br]
This changes only the [i]TTL presented to clients[/i]; it does not keep entries longer in the internal cache unless your cache policy allows it.[br]
If your upstream uses very short TTLs for fast changes/rotation, clamping may delay client-side visibility of those changes.
</enforce_user_dns_ttl_explain>

<NetIpv4TcpMtuProbing>TCP MTU probing</NetIpv4TcpMtuProbing>
<NetIpv4TcpMtuProbing_explain>[b]TCP MTU probing - Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD)[/b] is a method that allows the server to detect the MTU of the client.[br]
This is useful when the client is behind a NAT or firewall, and the server cannot send packets larger than the MTU.[br]
When enabled, the server will send a small packet to the client and wait for a response.[br]If the response is larger than the MTU, the server will adjust the MTU accordingly.[br]
If the client does not respond, the server will use the default MTU (1500 bytes).[br]
If the client responds, the server will use the MTU reported by the client.
</NetIpv4TcpMtuProbing_explain>

<rpfilter_0>The kernel does not check if the incoming packet’s source IP is reachable through the interface it arrived on.[br]Allows asymmetric routing and multi-homing setups.[br]Less secure, because spoofed IP packets can enter the system.[b]Used when complex routing requires flexibility.[/b]
</rpfilter_0>
<rpfilter_1>The kernel checks if the packet’s source IP is reachable only through the receiving interface.[br]If the route does not match, the packet is dropped.[br]Provides strong anti-spoofing protection.[br]Can break asymmetric routing or multi-WAN setups.[br][b]Recommended for simple, single-path networks.[/b]</rpfilter_1>
<rpfilter_2>The kernel checks if the source IP is reachable through any interface, not just the one it came from.[br]If reachable somewhere, the packet is accepted.[br]More flexible than strict mode, works with asymmetric routing.[br]Still filters obviously spoofed IP addresses.[br][b]            Recommended for routers, firewalls, and multi-WAN environments.[/b]</rpfilter_2>

[i]If the DNS Cache service is not installed, it will be automatically deployed.[br]
System-level name resolution (such as Active Directory) will always use the DNS settings defined in the system DNS tab.[/i]
</hacluster_use_local_dns_service_explain>

<urisblock_explain>Define here a request URI rule to be blocked.[br]
Each record is evaluated against the requested URI path.[br]
You can enter either an exact URI path or a regular expression (regex).[br][br]
Exact paths provide the best performance.[br]
Regular expressions allow advanced matching (patterns, prefixes, file types).[br][br]
When a rule matches, the request is immediately blocked.[br]
The connection is closed using the HTTP 444 return code, with no response body.[br][br]
Matching is case-sensitive and applies only to the URI path.</urisblock_explain>

<hotspot_ident_1>Associates the identified proxy session with the IP address of the machine connecting to the proxy.[br]
This method must be used with caution because if DHCP lease times are shorter than HotSpot session durations, users may be randomly authenticated under another user’s account.[br]
If users are behind NAT, the proxy will only see a single IP address (the firewall’s address), and user identification cannot be properly assigned.</hotspot_ident_1>
<hotspot_ident_2>Associates the identified proxy session with the MAC address of the machine connecting to the proxy.[br]This method must be used with caution because if clients are using different VLANs, the ARP protocol that transmits the MAC address is disrupted. In this case, the MAC address appears as 00:00:00:00:00:00, making it impossible to associate the session with user credentials.[br]
If IP address-based identification is enabled, an automatic fallback to IP address association will be performed.</hotspot_ident_2>

<decisionIPHoneypotAbout>Honeypot is a security feature designed to simulate listening ports across commonly targeted protocols within a controlled security environment.[br]
These ports are not bound to any real application; however, they actively monitor connection attempts and trigger events when a remote host initiates communication with services that are intentionally unused.[br]
Any node exhibiting suspicious or exploratory behavior (“overly curious”) is automatically blacklisted for a duration of three hours, and the incident telemetry is immediately reported to the DecisionIP central intelligence engine for correlation and reputation analysis.</decisionIPHoneypotAbout>

<slow_storage_detected_on>Slow storage detected on</slow_storage_detected_on>
<slow_storage_explain>The system has detected abnormal disk latency on %s.[br]
This condition is causing high I/O wait times which directly increases the system load average, even when CPU usage is low.[br]
[b]This is not necessarily a software problem[/b].[br]
Before investigating application-level causes, check the underlying storage infrastructure:[br][br]
[b]Virtual Machines (VMware, KVM, Hyper-V, Proxmox)[/b][br]
[br]- The VM datastore may be oversubscribed — too many VMs competing for the same physical disk
[br]- Thin-provisioned disks are slower than thick/eager-zeroed disks
[br]- The backing storage (NFS, iSCSI, local RAID) may be degraded or saturated
[br]- The virtual SCSI controller type matters — use paravirtual (pvscsi for VMware, virtio for KVM) instead of LSI Logic
[br]- Live storage migration or snapshot consolidation running in the background can cause temporary I/O stalls
[br]- Check the hypervisor host's own I/O wait — if the host is slow, all guests are slow.
[br][br]
[b]Physical Servers[/b]
[br]- A RAID array may be rebuilding after a disk replacement
[br]- A failing disk causes retries that spike latency before the disk is marked dead
[br]- Battery-backed write cache (BBU) in learning cycle disables write-back caching temporarily
[br]- HDD-based storage with mixed workloads (sequential + random) performs poorly — consider SSD or NVMe
</slow_storage_explain>
<optimizations_for_vm>Optimizations for Virtual machines</optimizations_for_vm>
<optimizations_for_vm_exp>Artica has detected that your virtualization system can achieve better performance by applying system optimizations</optimizations_for_vm_exp>
<optimizations_for_vm_perform>By clicking on button, Artica will:[br]
- Eliminates double scheduling of disk operations — Both the virtual machine and the host attempt to optimize disk I/O. When done simultaneously, they interfere with each other. This optimization ensures only the host handles disk scheduling.[br]
- Informs the system that the disk is non-rotational — Virtual disks have no physical read/write head, yet the OS may still apply HDD optimizations. This removes unnecessary read grouping and improves efficiency.[br]
- Reduces unnecessary background overhead on disk operations — By default, every I/O contributes to the system entropy pool. On busy systems, this creates measurable overhead with no real benefit. This optimization disables that behavior.[br]
- Optimizes write buffering behavior — Instead of allowing large write buffers to accumulate in memory, the system flushes smaller batches more frequently. This prevents sudden I/O stalls and improves responsiveness.[br]
- Releases unused file metadata more aggressively — Systems handling many small files (e.g., databases) may accumulate inode/dentry cache. This optimization frees unused entries sooner, reducing memory pressure.[br]
[br]
These changes are applied immediately and persist across reboots.[br]
[br]
[b]When is this needed?[/b][br]
[br]
These optimizations are only applied when the system is detected as a virtual machine (VMware, KVM, Hyper-V, etc.). Physical servers are not affected.[br]
[br]
If you experience high system load, slow response times, or see a "Slow storage detected" warning in the dashboard, applying these optimizations typically resolves the issue without requiring hardware changes.
</optimizations_for_vm_perform>

<temporaryFailureTTL>Negative-response cache TTL</temporaryFailureTTL>
<temporaryFailureTTL_explain>How long DNS caches upstream failures (SERVFAIL, REFUSED, timeouts).[br]
A single dropped packet from an upstream resolver creates one of these entries — the TTL determines how long that "failure" sticks before a fresh attempt is made.[br]
Recommended: 30 seconds.[br]
The legacy default of 3600 (1 hour) means one transient upstream glitch can keep returning errors to your users for the full hour,even if the upstream recovered seconds later.[br]
Set to 0 to disable negative caching entirely (every failure is retried immediately, with corresponding upstream load).
</temporaryFailureTTL_explain>

<check_url_explain>The full URL to probe, including scheme (e.g. https://www.microsoft.com).[br]
QuickCheck issues a GET against this URL through the LOCAL, PARENT and/or DIRECTpaths enabled below and measures DNS / TCP / TLS / TTFB / TOTAL phases plus jitter.
[br]Choose a sentinel that is reachable from all enabled paths and stable over time — a redirect chain or a frequently-rebuilt landing page will produce noisy latency numbers.[br]
Avoid endpoints that require authentication or POST data; only the response timing is recorded, not the body. </check_url_explain>
<run_local_explain>Probe this URL through the proxy instance running on this server (the LOCAL path, http://127.0.0.1:PORT).
[br]This is the most important path to enable — it measures what your end-users actually experience when going through the local proxy, including the cost of ACLs, SSL bumping, authentication and the parent-proxy hop if any.
[br]Disable only if this server has no local proxy (pure orchestration host).</run_local_explain>
<run_parent_explain>Probe this URL through the upstream parent proxy declared on the zone (the PARENT path, e.g. http://10.5.1.7:3128).
[br]Use it to isolate where slowness lives: if LOCAL is slow but PARENT is fast, the local proxy is the culprit;
[br]if both are slow, the issue is upstream (network, parent proxy, or Internet).
[br]Requires a valid parent_proxy on the zone — leaving it empty silently skips this path with a warning in the log.</run_parent_explain>
<run_direct_explain>Probe this URL with no proxy at all — a direct outbound HTTPS request from this server (the DIRECT path).[br]
Use it as the baseline: if DIRECT is fast but LOCAL is slow, the proxy chain adds the latency;
[br]if DIRECT is also slow, the issue is the network or the target itself.
[br]Only enable on hosts that actually have outbound Internet access without going through a proxy — in a DMZ or air-gapped network this will time out and pollute the verdict with UPSTREAM_FAIL.</run_direct_explain>

<quickcheck_thresholds_explain>These thresholds control how QuickCheck classifies each measurement as OK / WARN / CRIT.[br]
Two values are defined per metric — the WARN level (orange in the report,signals a degradation worth watching) and the CRIT level (red, signals an active incident).
[br]The verdict shown next to each check is computed from the TOTAL time of two comparable paths (typically LOCAL vs DIRECT, or LOCAL vs PARENT): both above WARN means generalized slowness, only LOCAL above WARN points to the local proxy.
[br]The phase thresholds (DNS / TCP / TLS / TTFB) and the JITTER thresholds are only used to color individual segments in the report — they do not influence the overall verdict. Defaults are calibrated for a typical corporate proxy on a healthy WAN;
[br]tighten them on fast LAN-only setups, loosen them on high-latency satellite or international links.[br]
Setting any value to zero or leaving it empty restores the default for that metric on the next save.</quickcheck_thresholds_explain>

<insecure_host_explain>Fully-qualified hostname to add to the insecure allow-list — no scheme, no port, no path.

Matching is exact: a wildcard or sub-domain entry is not supported, you must list each host individually.[br]
The hostname is compared case-sensitive against the host part of the probed URL, so use the same form you put in the check's URL field.
[br]Once added, every check whose target host matches this entry will be probed with TLS verification disabled and will be tagged with an orange badge in the report — confirming the certificate problem is intentional, not a silent regression.</insecure_host_explain>
<quickcheck_global_explain>Global parameters that apply to every probe issued by QuickCheck, regardless of zone or check.[br]
They cap how long a single HTTP request is allowed to take — both the initial TCP/TLS connection phase and the full request/response cycle.
[br]Tuning them affects every measurement and every verdict: too low and slow-but-working sites are flagged as upstream failures;
[br]too high and a single broken target stalls the whole run for minutes.[br]Defaults (4 s connect, 12 s total) are calibrated for typical corporate WAN sentinels;[br]raise them for international or satellite links, lower them on fast LAN-only setups where you want fast feedback.</quickcheck_global_explain>
<quickcheck_connect_timeout_explain>Maximum time allowed to establish the underlying TCP connection (and the TLS handshake when probing through a proxy CONNECT tunnel) before the probe gives up with a connection error.
[br]Keep it short — 3 to 6 seconds is enough on any reasonable network — because a stalled connect almost always means the target or proxy is unreachable, not that it is merely slow.
[br]Lower values give faster feedback when an upstream is down;
[br]higher values reduce false UPSTREAM_FAIL verdicts on links with very high RTT (intercontinental, satellite).
[br]Default: 4 seconds.</quickcheck_connect_timeout_explain>
<quickcheck_max_time_explain>Maximum total time allowed for the whole HTTP transaction — DNS, TCP, TLS, request, response body — before the probe is aborted.
[br]It MUST be larger than the connect_timeout (typically 2 to 4 times) and larger than the highest CRIT threshold you expect to read,otherwise legitimate slow responses get cut off and recorded as UPSTREAM_FAIL instead of being measured as critical-but-completed.
[br]Default: 12 seconds — fine for most sentinel pages;
[br]raise it if you intentionally probe heavy landing pages or high-latency targets.</quickcheck_max_time_explain>

<quickcheck_explain_checks>A check is a single sentinel target that QuickCheck probes on every run — typically a public or internal URL whose availability and response time reflect the health of a given route.[br]
Each check belongs to exactly one zone (which provides the local and parent proxy URLs to use) and declares which of the three paths (LOCAL / PARENT / DIRECT) should be measured against it.[br]
On every run, the configured paths are exercised in turn and the per-phase timings (DNS / TCP / TLS / TTFB / TOTAL) plus jitter are stored as one row in the SQLite database.
Pick targets that are stable over time (avoid endpoints that redirect or change frequently), reachable from all enabled paths, and representative of the kind of traffic your users actually generate — for example a CDN-hosted public site, an internal portal, and a third-party SaaS you depend on.</quickcheck_explain_checks>

<open_resolver_mode_explain>The DNS service accepts queries from any source IP (0.0.0.0/0) instead of only trusted networks and the entries listed in the Allowed networks.[br]
Use this only when the DNS server is intentionally exposed as a public resolver, and an upstream firewall already filters who can reach UDP/TCP port 53.[br]
Leaving this enabled on an Internet-facing host makes the server usable as a DNS amplification reflector — attackers send small queries with a forged source address, and your server sends the much larger response to the victim.[br]
A 1 Gbps line can be turned into ~60 Gbps of attack traffic.</open_resolver_mode_explain>

<strict_deny_exceptions_explain>Exceptions are carve-outs that re-allow traffic that this rule would otherwise block.[br]
An exception applies only when both its source and destination match the request. For example: deny all traffic from 10.189.17.0/25 except to google.com, but allow 10.189.17.109 to access test.domain.net.[br]
When an exception matches, the proxy service permits the request because the allow rule is evaluated before the deny rule. Therefore, the exception takes precedence over this rule and any later deny rule.[br]
[b]Note[/b]: Leave the source or destination empty to match any value. An exception with both source and destination empty is ignored.</strict_deny_exceptions_explain>

<smtp_sender_security_explain>Audits whether this mail server is correctly identified as a legitimate outbound SMTP sender.[br]
It checks the full sender-identity chain — HELO/hostname, outbound IP, forward and reverse DNS (FCrDNS), SPF, DKIM, DMARC, TLS, open-relay protection and sender ownership — then scores the result and lists prioritized fixes to improve deliverability and prevent spoofing.[br]
Read-only: it never changes your SMTP configuration.
</smtp_sender_security_explain>

<smtp_sender_login_maps_help>Restricts which authenticated users are allowed to send mail as a given sender address.[br]

<postscreen_explain_non_smtp_command_action>What postscreen does when a client sends non-SMTP commands (e.g. HTTP GET/POST) to the SMTP port — a strong bot signal. drop hangs up, enforce rejects, ignore logs.</postscreen_explain_non_smtp_command_action>
<postscreen_explain_bare_newline_action>What postscreen does when a client uses invalid bare line endings (LF without CR), which standards-compliant mail clients never do.</postscreen_explain_bare_newline_action>
<postscreen_explain_cache_map>Where postscreen stores per-client test results so already-vetted clients skip the tests on their next connection. Leave the default unless you know you need to change it.</postscreen_explain_cache_map>
<postscreen_explain_dnsbl_action>What postscreen does when a client's combined DNSBL score reaches the threshold below: enforce rejects, drop hangs up, ignore only logs the score.</postscreen_explain_dnsbl_action>
<postscreen_explain_dnsbl_threshold>The minimum combined DNSBL score (sum of the matched per-list weights) required before the DNSBL action is applied.</postscreen_explain_dnsbl_threshold>
<postscreen_explain_dnsbl_sites>The DNSBL/RBL reputation lists used to score the sending IP, one per line. Append *weight to give a list more influence, e.g. zen.spamhaus.org*3. A local DNS resolver/cache is strongly recommended.</postscreen_explain_dnsbl_sites>
<postscreen_explain_access_add>Add a network or host that is always allowed to bypass all postscreen tests (permit) or always rejected before SMTP processing (reject). A single IP is normalized to /32 (IPv4) or /128 (IPv6).</postscreen_explain_access_add>
<postscreen_explain_access_import>Paste a list of networks, one per line as "&lt;cidr&gt; [permit|reject] [# description]". Lines without an action default to permit; already-present networks are skipped.</postscreen_explain_access_import>

<about_articafile_share>[b]Artica File Sharing[/b] lets you run several fully isolated [b]Samba[/b] file servers on a single appliance.[br]Each [b]instance[/b] is bound to its own dedicated [b]IP address[/b] on a network interface, so it behaves like a separate physical file server on the network.[br]The instances are isolated from one another through [b]Linux network namespaces[/b], giving each one its own network stack, configuration tree, and data directory.[br]Every instance is supervised directly by the daemon [b]without systemd[/b], and a watchdog automatically restarts any process that stops unexpectedly.[br]You can create three kinds of instances: a [b]standalone server[/b], an [b]Active Directory domain controller[/b], or a [b]domain member[/b] joined to an existing directory.[br]Each instance manages its own [b]shared folders[/b], with fine-grained control over guest access, read and write permissions, and advanced options such as recycle bin, shadow copies, and full audit.[br][b]Users and groups[/b] can be backed by a local database, an OpenLDAP directory, or Active Directory, depending on the selected mode.[br]Windows clients discover each instance automatically through [b]NetBIOS[/b] and [b]WS-Discovery[/b], each advertised under its own name.[br][b]Live monitoring[/b] reports the status, memory usage, process identifier, uptime, and network address of every running instance in real time.[br]Because the instances are independent, you can [b]start, stop, restart, or reconfigure[/b] one of them without affecting any of the others.</about_articafile_share>

<auditd_cis_title>CIS hardening</auditd_cis_title>
<auditd_cis_form_explain>These directives are read by the CIS benchmark scanner in /etc/audit/auditd.conf, and the rule set covers CIS controls 4.1.3 to 4.1.16. Values that still hold their Debian factory setting are treated as unconfigured and are realigned automatically; any other value is considered a deliberate administrator choice and is preserved.</auditd_cis_form_explain>
<auditd_cis_space_left_action>Action when disk space runs low</auditd_cis_space_left_action>
<auditd_cis_space_left_action_explain>What auditd does when free space in the audit log partition drops below the space_left threshold. CIS requires email, which notifies the account below instead of only writing to syslog.</auditd_cis_space_left_action_explain>
<auditd_cis_action_mail_acct>Notification account</auditd_cis_action_mail_acct>
<auditd_cis_action_mail_acct_explain>Account notified when the disk space action is email. The CIS scanner expects the literal value root; a fully qualified address such as root@example.org is valid for auditd but fails the control.</auditd_cis_action_mail_acct_explain>
<auditd_cis_admin_space_left_action>Action at the critical threshold</auditd_cis_admin_space_left_action>
<auditd_cis_admin_space_left_action_explain>What auditd does when free space reaches the critical admin_space_left threshold. CIS requires halt, which powers the machine off. Artica defaults to single instead, which is less brutal on a production appliance but leaves the CIS control reported as failed.</auditd_cis_admin_space_left_action_explain>
<auditd_cis_max_log_file_action>Action when a log file is full</auditd_cis_max_log_file_action>
<auditd_cis_max_log_file_action_explain>What auditd does when an audit log reaches its maximum size. CIS requires keep_logs, which never deletes an audit trail. Watch free space on /var/log/audit: with keep_logs the number of retained logs is no longer capped.</auditd_cis_max_log_file_action_explain>
<auditd_cis_best_practices>CIS rule set</auditd_cis_best_practices>
<auditd_cis_best_practices_explain>Installs about forty audit rules covering CIS controls 4.1.3 to 4.1.16: time changes, account and group edits, network settings, MAC policy, logins and sessions, permission changes, failed file access, mounts, deletions, sudoers and sudo usage, and kernel module loading. Without them the scanner reports each rule as missing.</auditd_cis_best_practices_explain>
<auditd_cis_managed>Keep compliance enforced</auditd_cis_managed>
<auditd_cis_managed_explain>Artica rechecks these directives and the rule set every five minutes and restores them if they drift, for instance after an auditd package upgrade rewrites its configuration. This option turns itself off as soon as you pick a value that departs from the CIS target, so your own choice is never overwritten.</auditd_cis_managed_explain>
<auditd_cis_immutable>Immutable configuration</auditd_cis_immutable>
<auditd_cis_immutable_explain>Appends the -e 2 rule, which locks the audit configuration: no rule can be added, changed or removed until the next reboot. Enable it only once the rest of the configuration is settled.</auditd_cis_immutable_explain>
<auditd_cis_immutable_active>The audit configuration is immutable. No rule can be changed until the machine is rebooted.</auditd_cis_immutable_active>

<conntrack_not_engaged>Connection tracking is not engaged</conntrack_not_engaged>
<conntrack_not_engaged_explain>The kernel is not tracking any connection, so every chart on this page stays at zero. Loading the nf_conntrack module is not enough: since Linux 4.7 the kernel only registers its tracking hooks once a firewall rule asks for them. This appliance has a stateless ruleset (no conntrack match and no NAT table), so nothing ever requests tracking. Artica normally installs a dedicated rule for this; check that DisableConntrackTracking is not set to 1.</conntrack_not_engaged_explain>
<conntrack_tracking_opted_out>Connection tracking was turned off by an administrator (DisableConntrackTracking=1). The kernel does not track connections, so this page has no data to display. Set that setting back to 0 to collect statistics again, at the cost of one kernel tracking entry per network flow.</conntrack_tracking_opted_out>

<connection_tracking>Connection tracking</connection_tracking>
<connection_tracking_explain>Controls whether the Linux kernel tracks network connections. Tracking is what feeds the conntrackd dashboard (active connections, traffic, top talkers), and any stateful firewall rule needs it. It costs one kernel entry per network flow, so it can be given up on an appliance that only runs a stateless ruleset.</connection_tracking_explain>
<disable_connection_tracking>Disable connection tracking</disable_connection_tracking>
<disable_connection_tracking_explain>When turned on, Artica removes the dedicated firewall rule that makes the kernel track connections, and the conntrackd dashboard is left with no data to display. Leave it off unless you want to reclaim the memory used by the tracking table.</disable_connection_tracking_explain>

Everything else still applies to them: blocklists, HELO and sender checks, and the antivirus and antispam filters.</postfix.auth.whitelist.intro>

<unclassified_rejects>Unclassified blocks</unclassified_rejects>

<inbound_flow_intro>The filters a message crosses on its way in, in the order it meets them: postscreen sorts connections before the queue, the gateway and IP reputation decide while the session is open, and the anti-spam scores what has already been accepted. Pick the stage you need to inspect.</inbound_flow_intro>
<postfix_incoming_postscreen_explain>The first sorting stage, before the mail queue. It weeds out zombies and mass senders on their SMTP behaviour (premature greeting, blacklisted address, protocol tests) and closes the connection: what it turns away never becomes a message.</postfix_incoming_postscreen_explain>
<postfix_incoming_ksmg_explain>Kaspersky Secure Mail Gateway, wired as a milter. It inspects the message while the session is still open — antivirus, anti-phishing, content rules — and can refuse it before the sender hangs up.</postfix_incoming_ksmg_explain>
<postfix_incoming_rbl_explain>Reputation of the sending IP address, checked against public DNS blocklists. A listed address is refused at the start of the session, before the message is transmitted.</postfix_incoming_rbl_explain>
<postfix_incoming_rspamd_explain>Content anti-spam. It scores an accepted message on its headers, body, signatures and statistics, then marks it, quarantines it or rejects it depending on the score.</postfix_incoming_rspamd_explain>
<iptables_addons_not_installed>iptables add-ons are not installed</iptables_addons_not_installed>
<iptables_addons_not_installed_explain>The transparent TCP-to-proxy redirector relies on the Artica iptables add-ons, which ship the redsocks2 daemon. This package is not a Debian package, so it does not appear in the system package list, and without it the redirector cannot start. Install the iptables add-ons from the software updates section, then start the service again.</iptables_addons_not_installed_explain>

<send_history>Send the history</send_history>
<siem_history_title>Send the message history to the SIEM</siem_history_title>
<siem_history_explain>The appliance forwards new messages to the SIEM as they close, but the mail it already holds only reaches the SIEM at the pace of a background pass. This transfer hands the stored history over in one go: messages and refusals, batch after batch, until nothing is left. Live traffic keeps priority — the transfer waits whenever the outbound queue is busy, and never loses an event.</siem_history_explain>
<siem_history_mode_finish>Finish the outstanding transfer</siem_history_mode_finish>
<siem_history_mode_finish_explain>Hand over everything the SIEM has not acknowledged yet, over the whole stored history. Nothing already sent is sent again, and no period is needed. This is the ordinary choice, in particular right after connecting a SIEM.</siem_history_mode_finish_explain>
<siem_history_mode_resend>Send a period again</siem_history_mode_resend>
<siem_history_mode_resend_explain>Repeat a named period even if it was already sent — for a SIEM that was reinstalled or lost its data. The period is mandatory. The ordinary progress is not affected: what follows the period will not be sent a second time.</siem_history_mode_resend_explain>

<docker_rbac_your_account>Your account</docker_rbac_your_account>
<docker_rbac_how_title>Who is allowed to use Docker</docker_rbac_how_title>
<docker_rbac_how_explain>The Docker Manager daemon grants rights from its own file, /etc/artica/docker-rbac.json.[br]This file maps an account name to a list of Docker permissions, listed in the Permissions tab.[br]The Manager login is sent to the daemon as "Manager"; any other Web console account is sent under its own user id.[br]An account missing from this file is refused on every Docker page, even if it is an Artica administrator.[br]To grant access, edit the file as root and add an entry such as "jdoe": ["DOCKER_CONTAINER_VIEW", "DOCKER_CONTAINER_LOGS"], or ["DOCKER_ADMIN"] for full control.[br]Then restart the Docker Manager service: the file is only read when the daemon starts.</docker_rbac_how_explain>

<docker_run_command>Run a command</docker_run_command>
<docker_run_command_explain>Runs one command inside the container and shows its output and exit code.[br]The command runs through /bin/sh, unless you choose to run it without a shell.[br]It is stopped after the timeout (60 seconds at most), and each output is limited to 256 KB.[br]It is not an interactive terminal: a command waiting for keyboard input ends with the timeout.[br]Every command is recorded in the Docker audit log.</docker_run_command_explain>

<sata_ncq>SATA command queuing (NCQ)</sata_ncq>
<sata_ncq_explain>NCQ lets the system send up to 32 read and write commands at once to a SATA disk.[br]Some SSDs, often unbranded models, freeze while processing this queue.[br]The system then waits about 40 seconds, resets the disk link and loses the pending writes.[br]After such an error the system partition switches to read-only and services stop.[br]Disabling NCQ sends one command at a time, which avoids this firmware fault.[br]The cost is a lower throughput under heavy load, usually invisible on an appliance.[br]The change is applied immediately and kept at every boot through the GRUB boot loader.[br]It does not repair a worn disk: plan to replace a disk that keeps failing.</sata_ncq_explain>
<ncq_recommended>Recommended: this disk failed queued commands, see the kernel log.</ncq_recommended>

<quarantine_from_mismatch_explain>The address shown to the reader (header From) is compared with the sender declared during the SMTP session (envelope). When their domains differ and the displayed domain is not proven by DMARC or an aligned DKIM signature, the message is held in the quarantine as a possible impersonation. The user can still receive it from the report. Bounces, authenticated users and subdomains of the same organisation are never held.</quarantine_from_mismatch_explain>

<infomail>Infomail</infomail>
<infomail_explain>Infomail detects newsletters and automatic notifications (shipping notices, alerts, receipts). These messages are not spam.[br]Each category has one action: none, tag or quarantine.[br]None delivers the message untouched and only adds the X-Artica-Category header, which an Outlook or Microsoft 365 rule can use to sort it into a folder.[br]Tag delivers the message with the X-Artica-Category header and, if the subject tag is enabled, the subject prefix.[br]Quarantine holds the message and lists it in the recipient digest.[br]The subject prefix modifies the message, so it breaks the sender's DKIM signature.[br]Domain overrides replace the global actions for one protected domain.</infomail_explain>

<smtphard.section.smuggling_explain>A sender can hide a second message inside the first one by ending lines with a bare line feed, which other servers read differently. <docker_vw_install_explain>Artica deploys Vaultwarden as the compose stack vaultwarden, ready to use.[br]It generates an HTTPS certificate for the host name you give, closes the public sign-up page and protects the /admin page with your administration token.[br]Only a hash of the token is kept: write it down now, it cannot be shown again.[br]The mail server is optional: without it, invite users from the /admin page.</docker_vw_install_explain>
<docker_vw_server>Server</docker_vw_server>
<docker_vw_hostname>Host name or IP address</docker_vw_hostname>
<docker_vw_hostname_explain>The name the clients will use to reach the server.[br]The certificate is valid for this name only.</docker_vw_hostname_explain>
<docker_vw_port_explain>HTTPS port opened on this server for the clients.</docker_vw_port_explain>
<docker_vw_admin_token>Administration token</docker_vw_admin_token>
<docker_vw_admin_token_explain>At least 16 characters.[br]It opens the /admin page, where users are invited.</docker_vw_admin_token_explain>
<docker_vw_smtp>Mail server (optional)</docker_vw_smtp>
<docker_vw_smtp_explain>Used for invitations, e-mail verification and two-step login by e-mail.[br]Leave the server empty to send no mail.</docker_vw_smtp_explain>
<docker_vw_smtp_host>SMTP server</docker_vw_smtp_host>
<docker_vw_smtp_security>Connection security</docker_vw_smtp_security>
<docker_vw_smtp_plain>None (unencrypted)</docker_vw_smtp_plain>
<docker_vw_smtp_from>Sender address</docker_vw_smtp_from>
<docker_vw_done>Vaultwarden is being deployed</docker_vw_done>
<docker_vw_done_explain>The server starts in a few seconds: follow it from the stack window.[br]Download the certificate authority and install it on every computer and phone that uses the server.[br]In the Bitwarden applications, choose the self-hosted server and enter the address below.[br]Open the address followed by /admin with your token to invite the first users.</docker_vw_done_explain>
<docker_vw_next>Next step</docker_vw_next>
<docker_vw_follow>Open the stack</docker_vw_follow>
<docker_vw_follow_explain>State, health, logs and settings of the Vaultwarden server.</docker_vw_follow_explain>

<mpx_rule_title>Multipath selection rule</mpx_rule_title>
<mpx_rule_ecmp>Linux spreads the connections over the gateways in proportion to their weight. All the packets of one connection use the same gateway, chosen from</mpx_rule_ecmp>
<mpx_hash_l3>the source and destination addresses (L3 hash).</mpx_hash_l3>
<mpx_hash_l4>the addresses and the ports (L4 hash).</mpx_hash_l4>
<mpx_neigh_on>A gateway whose ARP resolution fails is skipped.</mpx_neigh_on>
<mpx_neigh_off>Linux does not check the gateways: an unreachable gateway keeps receiving its share of the connections.</mpx_neigh_off>
<mpx_rule_priority>systemd-networkd installs one default route per gateway, with the weight as metric: the gateway with the lowest weight carries all the traffic, the others take over only when its route disappears. The interface gateway is not used.</mpx_rule_priority>

<mir_banner_title>Traffic copy by the kernel (iptables TEE)</mir_banner_title>
<mir_banner>The kernel clones each IPv4 packet received or sent by</mir_banner>
<mir_banner2>and hands the copy to the destination address. The original packet continues unchanged. The probe receives packets addressed to other hosts: it must capture them and must not route them, otherwise every packet reaches its destination twice.</mir_banner2>

<rdpproxy_policy_web_route>Route of web targets</rdpproxy_policy_web_route>

<netagents_dhcp_scopes_explain>A scope is identified by its network (CIDR).[br]Each node places it on the interface that already serves this network, otherwise on the first interface whose IPv4 address belongs to this network.[br]Not defined: each node keeps its own scopes.[br]Defined: as soon as at least one scope of the policy is placed on a node, the policy replaces the local scopes of the matching interfaces, and a local scope that the policy does not contain is removed.[br]Defined but empty, or with no scope in the networks of a node: there is nothing to place, and the node keeps all its local scopes.[br]Emptying a policy therefore does not stop DHCP on a node: detach the policy, then change the scopes in the console of the node.[br]An interface of the node without an IPv4 address keeps its local scope.[br]Fixed reservations, relays and the MAC members of the pools stay local on each node.[br]</netagents_dhcp_scopes_explain>

<hcdx_title>Diagnosis of the error</hcdx_title>
<hcdx_intro>Artica read the Kerberos trace of the failed test and explains it below, most important first.[br]Principal tested:</hcdx_intro>
<hcdx_todo>What to do:</hcdx_todo>
<hcdx_trace>From the trace:</hcdx_trace>
<hcdx_sev_error>Error</hcdx_sev_error>
<hcdx_sev_warning>Warning</hcdx_sev_warning>
<hcdx_sev_info>Information</hcdx_sev_info>
<hcdx_spn_as_client_t>The test used a service name as its login</hcdx_spn_as_client_t>
<hcdx_spn_as_client_s>The check logged in with %s.[br]Active Directory never accepts a service name (SPN) as a login, so this error does not prove that the keytab is broken: the keytab also holds the computer account %s, which is the one to log in with.[br]</hcdx_spn_as_client_s>
<hcdx_spn_as_client_a>Test the keytab with the computer account.[br]If that works, the keytab is valid and only the check was wrong (fixed in Artica of 2026-11-15).[br]</hcdx_spn_as_client_a>
<hcdx_spn_not_mapped_t>No account uses this service name as its login</hcdx_spn_not_mapped_t>
<hcdx_spn_not_mapped_s>The keytab only holds the service name %s and no Active Directory account uses it as its login (userPrincipalName).[br]The keytab was exported without mapping it to a user, or the account was changed since.[br]</hcdx_spn_not_mapped_s>
<hcdx_spn_not_mapped_a>Export the keytab again with ktpass, mapping the service name to the service account (-mapuser sets the userPrincipalName), then import it.[br]</hcdx_spn_not_mapped_a>
<hcdx_account_not_found_t>The account does not exist in Active Directory</hcdx_account_not_found_t>
<hcdx_account_not_found_s>Active Directory does not know the account %s: it was deleted, renamed, or belongs to another domain.[br]</hcdx_account_not_found_s>
<hcdx_account_not_found_a>Check that the account exists in Active Directory Users and Computers, then join the cluster again or export a new keytab for the existing account.[br]</hcdx_account_not_found_a>
<hcdx_realm_mismatch_t>The keytab belongs to another domain</hcdx_realm_mismatch_t>
<hcdx_realm_mismatch_s>The keytab belongs to the realm %s but the cluster is configured for %s.[br]</hcdx_realm_mismatch_s>
<hcdx_realm_mismatch_a>Import the keytab of the right domain, or correct the Active Directory domain of the cluster.[br]</hcdx_realm_mismatch_a>
<hcdx_preauth_failed_t>The key of the keytab is out of date</hcdx_preauth_failed_t>
<hcdx_preauth_failed_s>Active Directory refuses the key of the keytab: the password of the account changed after the keytab was exported (password reset, keytab exported again on another machine, or the computer account renewed its password).[br]</hcdx_preauth_failed_s>
<hcdx_preauth_failed_a>Export a new keytab after the last password change, or join the cluster again, then import it.[br]Never run ktpass for the same account on two machines.[br]</hcdx_preauth_failed_a>
<hcdx_account_disabled_t>The account is disabled or locked</hcdx_account_disabled_t>
<hcdx_account_disabled_s>The account is disabled or locked out in Active Directory.[br]</hcdx_account_disabled_s>
<hcdx_account_disabled_a>Enable or unlock the account in Active Directory Users and Computers.[br]</hcdx_account_disabled_a>
<hcdx_password_expired_t>The password of the account has expired</hcdx_password_expired_t>
<hcdx_password_expired_s>The password of the account has expired.[br]</hcdx_password_expired_s>
<hcdx_password_expired_a>Set Password never expires on the service account, reset its password, then export and import a new keytab.[br]</hcdx_password_expired_a>
<hcdx_clock_skew_t>The clocks differ by more than 5 minutes</hcdx_clock_skew_t>

<hcdx_clock_skew_a>Enable Synchronize time with Active Directory or point NTP to a domain controller, then check again.[br]</hcdx_clock_skew_a>
<hcdx_kdc_unreachable_t>No domain controller answers</hcdx_kdc_unreachable_t>

<dhcprelay_option82>Relay agent information (option 82)</dhcprelay_option82>
<dhcprelay_option82_explain>The relay can add option 82 to each request it forwards.[br]It tells the DHCP server which interface the request came from (circuit ID) and which relay sent it (remote ID).[br]The server can then give an address per network port instead of per MAC address.[br]The relay removes the option from the server replies before sending them to the clients.</dhcprelay_option82_explain>
<dhcprelay_add_option82>Add option 82 to relayed requests</dhcprelay_add_option82>
<dhcprelay_add_option82_explain>Adds the relay agent information option to every request sent to the DHCP servers.[br]The remote ID and the circuit IDs are only sent when this is enabled.</dhcprelay_add_option82_explain>
<dhcprelay_policy>Requests that already carry option 82</dhcprelay_policy>
<dhcprelay_policy_explain>A client should never send option 82 itself.[br]Replacing it prevents a client from choosing its own circuit ID, and with it its address.[br]Keep it only for a trusted relay placed in front of this one.</dhcprelay_policy_explain>
<dhcprelay_policy_replace>Replace it with the option of this relay</dhcprelay_policy_replace>
<dhcprelay_policy_append>Keep it and add the option of this relay</dhcprelay_policy_append>
<dhcprelay_policy_forward>Forward the request unchanged</dhcprelay_policy_forward>
<dhcprelay_policy_discard>Drop the request</dhcprelay_policy_discard>
<dhcprelay_remote_id>Remote ID</dhcprelay_remote_id>
<dhcprelay_remote_id_explain>Identifies this relay for the DHCP server.[br]Choose the host name of the appliance, the address of the relay on the client network, or a fixed value.</dhcprelay_remote_id_explain>
<dhcprelay_rid_none>Not sent</dhcprelay_rid_none>

<dhcprelay_rid_custom>Fixed value</dhcprelay_rid_custom>
<dhcprelay_remote_id_value>Fixed remote ID</dhcprelay_remote_id_value>
<dhcprelay_remote_id_value_explain>Used only when the remote ID is a fixed value.[br]Write text, or bytes as hex:c0:ff:ee.[br]120 bytes at most.</dhcprelay_remote_id_value_explain>
<dhcprelay_circuit_ids>Circuit IDs per interface</dhcprelay_circuit_ids>
<dhcprelay_circuit_ids_explain>One line per interface, written interface=value, for example eth1=cabinet 3 or eth2=hex:00:03.[br]An interface without a line sends its name.[br]Only downstream interfaces of the relay are allowed, and two interfaces cannot share the same value.</dhcprelay_circuit_ids_explain>
